**Eight practitioner assumptions, each negated**

1. A conv downstream always gains more when its feeding edge is also a conv (more depth is better). If false, a conv fed by skip_connect gains more, because skip leaves clean features for the conv to use.
2. Pooling upstream just smooths features and costs little. If false, a conv after avg_pool gains less (redundant receptive field) or more (1x1 mixing restores what pooling lost), depending on kernel size.
3. A direct 0->3 shortcut is redundant once deeper conv paths exist. If false, the shortcut helps more when the other paths are deep, as a gradient-flow route.
4. Capacity is fungible, so a conv on any path substitutes for a conv on another. If false, same-type edits on parallel paths interact through scale mismatch at the summing node, not just saturation.
5. Adding a conv never hurts at the merge node. If false, a conv-heavy stream summed with an identity or pooled stream is mis-scaled, and the edit hurts.
6. Bigger kernels are better regardless of context. If false, 3x3 after pooling or beside 3x3 elsewhere loses, while 1x1 gains.
7. Skip_connect is a harmless, mildly helpful edit. If false, skip hurts when it routes a raw or pooled stream into a node that conv streams dominate.
8. Interactions are dataset-specific noise. If false, the same sign holds on all three datasets, because it is driven by trainability and effective depth, which are dataset-independent.

None of the hypotheses condition on the edited edge itself or on a parent set to none. Only two (edit 4 conv3x3 given edge 0 conv3x3, and edit 3 conv3x3 given edge 5 conv3x3) argue equivalent capacity.
